title: 道德經 第七十二章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 72, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 88. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 72 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 愛己 (Loving Oneself). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
民不畏威，
則大威至。
無狎其所居，
無厭其所生。

morph.gloss: the people, the common folk — the ruled, as against their ruler
to fear, to stand in awe of
awe — the dread that a ruler's power puts into men; majesty and terror in the one word
do not — 無 here is the prohibitive (the word usually written 毋), not the usual 'there is no'
to make free with, to press up against with no sense of distance — 狎 is 'to be over-familiar with'; the crowding the line needs is where it meets the variant reading 狹, see the note
that which —— : makes a noun of the verb that follows it
to dwell in, to settle in
to sate to the point of loathing, to press on until no more can be borne
to live, to make a living

sentences.l:
The people not fearing awe,
then the great awe arrives.
Do not crowd what they dwell in,
do not press on what they live by.
sentences.i: When the people no longer stand in awe of your power, then the great terror is on its way. Do not crowd the place where they live; do not press so hard on their livelihood that they cannot bear it.
sentences.n:
畏 and 威 are the two ends of one thing and were near-twins in sound as well (wèi, wēi): 畏 is the fearing, 威 is the thing feared — the dread that authority carries about with it. The line is about a ruler whose 威 has stopped working.

大威 is not more of the same. Wang Bi's comment ends 天誅將至, 'heaven's execution is on its way': when the people can no longer bear the ruler's terror, top and bottom collapse together and what arrives is a terror nobody wields. The chapter's first two lines are therefore a warning to the man holding the whip, not a threat to the people.

無 here is not the 無 you know from 無為 and 無名. It is the prohibitive — 'do not' — the word normally written 毋, for which 無 stands in constantly. Only the imperative context tells you which is meant.

Two honest uncertainties. 狎 is rare, and its own sense is 'to be over-familiar, to make free with'; some editions print 狹 xiá instead, 'to narrow, to cramp'. The crowding in the English here is where the two meet, and little turns on which is printed.

And 其 has no owner in the Chinese at all. English cannot say 'the dwelling' without deciding whose, so the standing rule in this book applies: where the text names no owner, take the nearer topic — here the 民 that opens the unit — and put the alternative in a note. The alternative is a strong one. Wang Bi glosses 居 as purity and stillness and 生 as humility and holding back, which makes the two lines a warning to the ruler about his own ground rather than about the people's houses. His paraphrase closes 言威力不可任也, 'it says that awe and force cannot be relied on', which is where both readings end up.

morph.gloss: to press on them, to weary them past bearing — the ruler is the one doing it here

sentences.l: Now, it is only that he does not press them,
sentences.n: The couplet is cut in half here because Wang Bi's commentary interrupts between the two clauses, and our sense-units follow his interruptions rather than a modern editor's. So you meet the 'because' and the 'therefore' of one sentence as two units, which is a fair picture of how the text reached us: with a commentator's voice already inside it.

morph.gloss: therefore, and so — a fused connective; neither half gives you it alone
to have had one's fill of him, to grow sick of him — now the people are the ones doing it

sentences.l: and so they do not have their fill of him.
sentences.i: and so they never grow sick of him.
sentences.n:
The same character twice, and it turns round between the two halves: in 夫唯不厭 the ruler is the one doing the 厭, in 是以不厭 the people are. Chinese marks neither subject and neither voice; the sentence is a hinge with nothing to show which way it swings but the sense.

厭 yàn is 'to have had one's fill', to be glutted to the point of loathing — the word from chapter 53's 厭飲食, sated with food and drink. Some readers take the first three occurrences as the different word 壓 yā, 'to press down on', which the character also writes; that gives 'oppress' outright rather than 'sate past bearing'. The reading kept here is yàn throughout, so the pivot stays visible: press a people until they are full of you, and they will be full of you.

morph.gloss: therefore, and so — a fused connective; neither half gives you it alone
the sage — in this book the ruler who holds the Way, not a moral saint
himself — the reflexive object stands BEFORE its verb, always
to show, to put on display (read xiàn, the causative of jiàn 'to see')

sentences.l: Therefore the sage knows himself and does not show himself,
sentences.n:
自見 is chapter 24's word — 自見者不明, 'one who shows himself is not bright' — and it carries the same two lessons: the reflexive 自 goes in front of its verb, where English wants the object after, and 見 read xiàn is the causative, to make appear, not jiàn 'to see'.

Set 自知 against 自見 and you have the chapter's turn. Knowing yourself is inward and costs the people nothing; showing yourself is the 威 of the opening lines in miniature, the display that presses on everyone who has to look at it.

morph.gloss: to love, to hold dear; classically also to be sparing of
to prize, to treat as costly — the adjective 'precious' working as a verb

sentences.l: loves himself and does not prize himself;
sentences.n: 愛 and 貴 look like the same attitude and are not. 愛 is care — and in classical usage it slides toward being sparing of a thing, not spending it. 貴 is valuation, setting a price on yourself and expecting it paid; it is the verb of chapter 13's 貴大患若身. To look after yourself without holding yourself dear is the whole distinction, and the chapter's traditional title, 愛己, takes its name from the first half of it.

morph.gloss: to put away, to leave behind — the classical sense, the reverse of modern Mandarin 'to go to'
that, the far thing — always set against 此
to take, to keep hold of

sentences.l: and so he puts that away and takes this.
sentences.n: The closing formula of chapters 12 and 38, and as always the text leaves 'that' and 'this' unfilled. Here they have just been named in the two lines above: 彼 is the showing and the prizing, 此 is the knowing and the loving. Near and far are moral directions in this book — what is 此 is at hand, inside, unremarkable.
